title: Shortest Round Trip for Coins
statement:
A tree has n nodes numbered 0 to n − 1, joined by the n − 1 undirected edges. coins[i] is 1 if node i holds a coin and 0 otherwise.

You pick any starting node. From wherever you stand you can grab every coin that is at most 2 edges away. You may also walk along an edge to a neighbour, which costs one step. You must collect every coin and finish back at the node you started from.

Return the fewest steps needed. Walking the same edge twice costs two steps.

examples.why: Start at 2: the coin on 0 is two edges away. Step to 3, grab the coin on 5, and step back to 2.
Standing on the centre, both coins are one edge away, so no walking is needed.
The branch 8–9–10 holds no coin, so it never needs a visit. Walk 2 → 5 and back: from 2 you reach the coin on 0, from 5 the coin on 7.

constraints: edges.length = n − 1, and the edges form a tree
hints: Some parts of the tree never need a visit at all. Which ones?
A leaf with no coin is useless: drop it. Doing that repeatedly removes every coinless branch. Now every leaf holds a coin, and you can grab it from two edges away.
After the coinless trim, peel off the leaves twice more. Whatever is left is the part you must walk; each of its edges is walked once out and once back.

explain.intuition:
The walk out and back covers a connected piece of the tree, and every edge of that piece is crossed exactly twice. So the question is: what is the smallest connected piece you must stand on?

First, a leaf without a coin is pointless to visit, and once it is gone its parent may become a coinless leaf too. Trim those away repeatedly, like pruning unused imports until nothing more falls off. Now every leaf has a coin. Since you can reach 2 edges, you never need to stand on a leaf or on the node just above it: peel off one layer of leaves, then one more. The nodes that survive must be visited, and visiting them is enough. The answer is 2 × (remaining nodes − 1), or 0 if at most one node remains.
steps: Build adjacency lists and the degree of every node.
Queue every leaf (degree 1) that has no coin. Pop, remove it, lower its neighbour's degree, and queue the neighbour if it just became a coinless leaf.
Twice: collect all remaining leaves at once, remove them together, and lower their neighbours' degrees.
Count the nodes still present. Return 2 × (count − 1) if count ≥ 1, else 0.
pitfalls: Peeling the two layers one leaf at a time with a queue. The second layer must be the leaves after the first layer is gone, not leaves created while you are still removing the first.
Peeling the two layers before removing coinless branches. A coinless leaf would then be treated as a coin you must reach.
Returning 2 × (nodes − 1) when no nodes are left, which gives −2.

solutions.title: Try every start
solutions.idea: Root the tree at each node. Each coin needs its ancestor two levels up (or the root) to be visited; the visited set is the union of paths from the root to those ancestors.

solutions.title: Trim coinless leaves, then peel two layers
solutions.idea: Remove coinless branches with a leaf queue, then remove all leaves twice in rounds. The survivors form the piece you must walk, each edge twice.

followups: The reach is d edges instead of 2. What changes in the algorithm?
You no longer have to return to the start. How would you adjust the answer?
